text.p: UnionAmerica Holdings Plc seeks to grow by making an acquisition in the U.S. surplus lines business, the company's chairman said on Wednesday.
Philip Marcell told Reuters that UnionAmerica would target a "high-quality" surplus lines insurer with premium volume of about $50 million.
He said the company already identified a few possibilities but it had not yet entered discussions with any of the prospective targets.
Marcell said potential targets must have at least $10 million in premium volume and not more than about $100 million.
He also said UnionAmerica was interested in forming a management services company in the United States to conduct regulatory reviews and audits of agents.
UnionAmerica would like to accomplish at least one of those actions this year, he said.
UnionAmerica intends to expand its U.S. surplus lines business, where it sees better growth prospects than in its professional liability treaty business, Marcell said.

Marcell, who is scheduled to give a presentation at a Merrill Lynch insurance conference in New York on Thursday, said he expected premium volume in its core professional liability reinsurance treaty business to stagnate in the United States.
"We don't see in our core casualty treaty business much growth," Marcell said.
"We've seen the growth in something we went into a few years back, which is the primary insurance surplus lines business here in the U.S.," he said.
"We have seen growth in the non-U.S. business as Europe, particularly, and certainly Australia has become more litigious."
He said he saw improved sales this year at UnionAmerica's Dutch auto insurance joint venture.
UnionAmerica expects to break even or turn a marginal profit on the Dutch venture in 1997, he said.
The venture with a Dutch motor trade organization, which sells auto insurance through telemarketing, expects to sell 50,000 policies in 1997, up from 25,000-30,000 in 1996, he said.
Marcell said London-based UnionAmerica was now approved as a surplus lines insurer in all but three U.S. jurisdictions.
UnionAmerica said it expected strong growth in its casualty surplus lines business this year, with premium volume rising to about $15 million from $8 million to 9 million in 1996, he said.
He also said it expected the property surplus lines business to grow slightly this year.
UnionAmerica, which derives about 86 percent of its business from the United States, also sees growth in its business outside that country over time, Marcell said.
UnionAmerica, which last month acquired a majority stake in Jago Dedicated Ltd, is now working to acquire a large minority stake in the associated managing agency.
U.S. broker Aon Corp has a minority stake in Jago Dedicated, the sole shareholder in Jago Capital Ltd, a dedicated Lloyd's of London corporate capital vehicle.
"We are doing with Aon due diligence on taking a very large minority interest in the associated Lloyd's managing agency," Marcell said.
He said he did not expect UnionAmerica to increase its participation in Lloyd's anytime soon.
